But the main problem with bank management is that they took a very, very risky position, the riskiest investment strategy you could take. They took all of those uninsured deposits and then they invested them in long dated hold to maturity securities, relatively safe securities, by the way, US treasuries and agency securities, mortgage backed securities. But the problem was they invested in those long duration bonds before the Federal Reserve started to tighten monetary policy. And so you had a precipitous increase in interest rates. And there was no hedging of that interest rate risk. And as a result, the value of those assets plummeted. They had unrealized losses. And when the tech sector, which was under duress, began to move money out of the bank. And when there were withdrawals, because the institution marked those assets to market, in the middle of last week and they realized they had all these unrealized losses, well then the bank had to actually sell those assets at a loss in order to cover all of the withdrawals. That caused a bank run that was simply unsustainable and that was what necessitated regulator intervention. But the underlying cause though is the more interesting part of the story, Sarah, because uh... this was a failure not just a bank management this was a failure of government policy it was a failure of bank supervision now you will get some progressives uh... including the president uh... elizabeth warren and others who blame uh... uh... regulatory reform for this but but let's be clear this was not a failure of existing bank regulation The regulators had all the tools that they needed to prevent this from happening. And in fact, over the weekend, when you saw Treasury, the FDIC, and the Fed intervene, they had the tools that they needed to limit the bank run and to address the systemic risk issue over the weekend. This was not a failure of a lack of regulation. This was a failure of bank supervision. And the San Francisco Fed was regulating and supervising this institution, SVB. They were in it. They had all the visibility that they needed. And they failed to address this growing liquidity challenge for this bank. And they failed to identify this interest rate risk that was growing. And it was hiding in plain sight. And the regulators simply were distracted by whatever else they were doing. and not focused on the nuts and bolts of banks supervision and then if you go back even further in the history of this you see a a failure a just breathtaking failure of government policy fiscal policy mistakes and monetary policy mistakes that created this interest rate sensitivity on the part of this bank and others uh... where you had uh... massive amounts of fiscal stimulus that was frankly propagate and unnecessary and fiscally reckless all of the spending coming out of Washington over the last several years, which created the highest inflation rate in 40 years. And monetary policy that was excessively loose and accommodative, that where quantitative easing was continuing well into an economic growth cycle, and where the Fed kept interest rates too low for too long, resulting in this inflation and massive growth in the money supply that necessitated a very precipitous abrupt change in policy and a tightening, the fastest tightening in monetary policy and rise in interest rates in decades. And when that happens, things are going to break. And this was an example of a precipitous rise in interest rates that created the stress on this bank that was loaded up in long duration hold to maturity securities where they, uh, with the assets plummeted in value.
